body.objective: Students will be able to explore the history of Chinese Canadians.
body.iCan: I can explore the history of Chinese Canadians.
successCriteria: I can describe key events in Chinese Canadian history
I can explain the head tax and the Chinese Immigration Act
I can explain why the history matters today
body.hook: Chinese Canadians helped build this country, including the Canadian Pacific Railway through the Rocky Mountains, while facing unfair laws for decades. Their history is part of Canada's history.

study.title: 华人在加拿大的历史
study.question: What is the history of Chinese Canadians?
study.passage:
Timeline (written for this lesson from public sources):
1858: Chinese miners arrive in British Columbia during the Fraser River gold rush.
1881–1885: thousands of Chinese labourers help build the Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR) through British Columbia's mountains. They did some of the most dangerous work for lower pay than other workers, and many died.
1885: once the railway was nearly finished, the federal government imposed a head tax on Chinese immigrants: $50, raised to $100 in 1900 and $500 in 1903, a huge sum at the time.
1923: the Chinese Immigration Act almost completely banned Chinese immigration. Chinese Canadians sometimes call 1 July 1923 "Humiliation Day."
1947: the act was repealed and Chinese Canadians gained the right to vote federally, partly in recognition of Chinese Canadians who served in the Second World War.
2006: the Government of Canada formally apologized for the head tax and offered redress.
Activity: groups build a bilingual timeline (English with Mandarin key words: 铁路, 人头税, 道歉) and discuss: Why is it important to remember unfair laws? What contributions did Chinese Canadians make?
study.source: Summary from public sources, including Government of Canada and museum records.
steps: Learn about the gold rush and railway
Learn about the 1923 act and its repeal
discussion: What work did Chinese labourers do on the CPR?
Why was the head tax unfair?
Why did the law change in 1947?
study.product: Create a bilingual timeline of six events in Chinese Canadian history and write a paragraph on why this history matters.

body.objective: Students will be able to explore Chinatowns and community life.
body.iCan: I can explore Chinatowns and community life.
successCriteria: I can describe the history and role of Chinatowns in Canada
I can describe community life and cultural organizations
I can name notable Chinese Canadians, including Albertans
body.hook: Chinatowns in Victoria, Vancouver, Calgary and Edmonton grew because Chinese Canadians built communities where they could support each other, keep their culture and run businesses, especially when laws kept them out of other places.

study.title: 唐人街和社区
study.question: What role do Chinatowns and communities play for Chinese Canadians?
study.passage:
Background (written for this lesson from public sources):
Victoria's Chinatown, founded in 1858, is the oldest in Canada. Vancouver's Chinatown is one of the largest in North America. Calgary's and Edmonton's Chinatowns date from the early 1900s.
Why Chinatowns grew: discrimination and laws limited where Chinese immigrants could live and work, so they built communities with shops, restaurants, family and clan associations, newspapers and schools to support one another.
Community life today: Chinese-language schools on weekends, lion dance teams, Lunar New Year parades, cultural centres, seniors' associations and businesses. Many Chinese Canadians now live across cities, and newer communities have grown in suburbs.
Notable Chinese Canadians: Douglas Jung, the first Chinese Canadian member of Parliament (1957); Adrienne Clarkson, Governor General of Canada (1999–2005); Normie Kwong, born in Calgary, a Canadian Football League star and Lieutenant Governor of Alberta (2005–2010).
Mandarin sentences: 卡尔加里有唐人街。唐人街有很多餐馆和商店。周末很多学生去中文学校。
Activity: groups research one Chinatown or community organization and present three facts with Mandarin key words.
study.source: Summary from public sources on Canadian Chinatowns and notable Chinese Canadians.

discussion: What does a Chinese-language school do?

body.objective: Students will be able to present on cultural heritage.
body.iCan: I can present on cultural heritage.
successCriteria: I can research an aspect of Chinese Canadian heritage or my own heritage
I can present it using Mandarin I've learned in grades 7–9
I can reflect on how heritage is kept alive
body.hook: Cultural heritage is what we inherit from our families and communities: languages, foods, stories, celebrations and values. In this final project, you'll present on cultural heritage in Mandarin and English.

study.title: 文化遗产
study.question: How is cultural heritage kept alive, and how can I present it in Mandarin?
study.passage:
Project guide (written for this lesson):
Choose one topic: a Chinese Canadian tradition (Lunar New Year in Calgary or Edmonton, lion dance, Chinese-language school, family recipes like dumplings), a part of Chinese Canadian history (railway workers, the head tax, a Chinatown), a notable Chinese Canadian, or your own family's heritage compared with a Chinese tradition.
Content (2–3 minutes): 1. 介绍 (introduce): 我要介绍… 2. What and where: facts (in English with Mandarin key words). 3. Why it's important: 我觉得…很重要, 因为… 4. How it's kept alive: 社区…, 学校…, 家人… 5. Reflection: what you learned in Mandarin 7–9: 我学到了…
Language goals: use at least ten Mandarin sentences, drawing on structures from grades 7–9 (有, 在, 会, 比, 因为…所以…, 都, 也).
Visuals: images and key characters.
Respect: present cultures and histories accurately; if interviewing family or community members, ask permission and thank them.
Rubric: content, Mandarin accuracy and range, pronunciation and tones, visuals, reflection.
study.source: Original project written for this lesson.
steps: Write ten Mandarin sentences using learned structures
Present and reflect on your learning
discussion: Why did you choose your topic?
How is this heritage kept alive?
Which Mandarin structures did you use?
What are you proudest of learning in Mandarin?
study.product: Present a 2–3 minute heritage presentation with at least ten Mandarin sentences, visuals and a reflection on your Mandarin learning.
